topics.title: 一站式查看 CKB Community Fund DAO 提案、投票与执行进展

recent_posts.topic_title: 一站式查看 CKB Community Fund DAO 提案、投票与执行进展
recent_posts.author: JackyLHH
recent_posts.content_text:
我想介绍一下用 AI 工具制作的 CKB Community Fund DAO Dashboard。构建这个网站主要是为了方便大家集中查看 DAO 的规则、提案、投票结果、执行进展与资金使用情况。
网址：
https://ckbcommunityfunddao.xyz
主要功能
实时抓取并整理 Nervos Talk、Metaforo 等公开来源的数据
浏览 DAO 提案及其当前状态
查看某个提案的概览、路线图、申请预算、投票结果和进展
追踪提案人发布的周报、里程碑报告与结项报告
按状态和提案类型搜索、筛选
支持中文和英文
提供邮件与 Telegram 订阅
AI 自动汇总每日提案动态
网站会自动检查过去 24 小时内出现的：
新发布的提案
现有提案的进展更新
AI 会识别和汇总这些动态，并在每天北京时间约 16:00 自动发送邮件和 Telegram 订阅消息。只有出现新动态时才会发送，没有变化时不会打扰大家。
如何订阅
邮件订阅：
https://ckbcommunityfunddao.xyz
网站最底部，提交邮箱后，需要打开收到的确认邮件并点击 “确认订阅”。如果没有在收件箱中看到，请检查垃圾邮件或 Spam 文件夹。
image11920×1071 167 KB
Telegram 中文频道：
Telegram
CKB Community Fund DAO 中文动态
You can view and join @CKBCommunityFundDAO_CN right away.
Telegram English Channel：
Telegram
CKB Community Fund DAO Updates
You can view and join @CKBCommunityFundDAO right away.
image21920×1284 370 KB
欢迎参与改进
网站仍在持续完善中。如果你发现数据错误、信息遗漏，或者对页面和订阅功能有建议，欢迎：
在本帖回复
在 GitHub 提交 Issue 或 Pull Request
GitHub：
github.com
GitHub - JackyLHH/ckb-community-fund-dao-dashboard: Community-maintained dashboard for CKB Community...
Community-maintained dashboard for CKB Community Fund DAO rules, proposals, voting, funding, and progress.
这是一个非官方的社区信息工具。自动抓取和 AI 汇总可能存在遗漏或判断错误，重要的提案状态、金额和投票结果，请同时回到 Nervos Talk、投票页面和链上记录进行核验。
希望这个网站能帮助大家更方便地了解和参与 CKB Community Fund DAO。感谢大家的使用、反馈与共同完善！
最后，我还想感谢 @zz_tovarishch 在构建网站过程中提供的宝贵建议和全力支持。

Keep reviewed bilingual overviews instead of re-parsing them into MyMemory (#2)
main ← chukwuma619:fix/keep-reviewed-milestone-overview
opened 05:32PM - 28 Sep 26 UTC
chukwuma619
+561
-823
## Summary
Production `/api/translation` returned 502 for proposal 10739 (Riv…et) because the live loader discarded the reviewed bilingual overview and sent a chopped Nervos Talk extract to MyMemory, which rejects any segment over 500 bytes.
- Live enrichment now keeps a proposal override `overview`. It may still fill a missing `budgetLabel` from the forum post, but it no longer replaces reviewed objectives or milestones. 10739 therefore keeps the reviewed Chinese and English milestone text and does not call `/api/translation`.
- If AI Gateway is unset and the source is over 500 bytes, `/api/translation` skips MyMemory and returns `{ ok: false, code: "public_query_too_long" }` with HTTP 200, so the page keeps the original language instead of failing.
- The committed snapshot now includes proposals 10736 and 10739.
## Test plan
- [ ] `npm test`
- [ ] Confirm proposal 10739 still has the reviewed bilingual milestones in `lib/proposal-overrides.ts`
- [ ] On a recent proposal with a reviewed overview, confirm live enrichment does not replace that overview
- [ ] Confirm a translation request over 500 bytes does not call MyMemory and does not return 502

topics.title: LS-IDL: a Lock Script Interface Description Language for CKB (derive, validate, commit)

recent_posts.topic_title: LS-IDL: a Lock Script Interface Description Language for CKB (derive, validate, commit)
recent_posts.author: OWK50GA
recent_posts.content_text:
TL;DR
Since my original CKB IDL post, the project has grown from a flat lock-witness prototype into a versioned interface protocol with working tooling:
IDL 0.1.0 now has a standalone specification, JSON Schema, canonical fixtures and conformance vectors.
The Rust derive supports wider integers, arbitrary fixed bytes, typed vectors, trailing optionals, nested structs, semantic types and explicitly tagged unions.
The Rust client verifies on-chain commitments, validates recursive documents, and decodes or encodes ordered witness objects with stable error paths.
Binding Trailer 1 replaces the old raw 32-byte suffix with a detectable, versioned 46-byte commitment.
The new ckb-idl CLI validates, binds, inspects and verifies deterministic deployment bundles without modifying source artifacts.
Six reference lock scripts now exercise hashes, signatures, vectors, optionals, nested fields and unions.
The project is being consolidated under the ckb-idl GitHub organization.
The next major step is completing end-to-end deployment evidence and building the script registry: an npm/OpenZeppelin/explorer-like discovery layer for verified IDLs, reusable scripts, deployment metadata and transaction-builder examples. Molecule integration remains on the roadmap rather than being replaced by IDL.
CKB IDL Update: Recursive Witnesses, a 0.1.0 Specification, Verified Clients, and Deployment Bundles
The original version was an experiment around a fairly narrow idea:
Rust witness struct
- derive an IDL
- append its hash to a script executable
- let wallets validate witness bytes before submission
Since then, I have spent time testing the idea against more realistic scripts, expanding the supported type system, separating the protocol from its implementations, and building the missing deployment tooling.
The project is now simply called CKB IDL rather than LS-IDL. IDL 0.1.0 still supports only WitnessArgs.Lock, but the longer-term direction includes other script interfaces, so “Lock Script IDL” had become unnecessarily restrictive.
This post is an update on what has changed, what now works, and what I intend building next.
The original problem
CKB scripts are highly programmable, but wallets and transaction builders do not have a standard machine-readable way to discover the witness format expected by an unfamiliar script. “Unfamiliar” in this context refers to a machine having access to nothing but the code hash of the code cell that holds the script.
This means that integration today requires prior knowledge of the script, and when this knowledge is wrong, errors are often discovered only during VM execution.
The goal of CKB IDL remains:
script identity
- discover interface
- verify interface against deployed code
- construct or inspect witness safely
The registry is used for discovery, but it is not trusted as the authority. The deployed code cell commits to the exact IDL bytes.
1. IDL Specification
The protocol is no longer defined implicitly by the Rust derive implementation. There is now a dedicated specification repository: https://github.com/ckb-idl/ckb-idl-spec
It defines:
The IDL 0.1.0 JSON Schema
The interfaces document model
The witness_args.lock interface
The ckb-idl-linear-0.1.0 encoding profile
Structural and semantic types
Nested structs and tagged unions
Optional-field behaviour
RFC 8785 canonicalization
Stable error categories are JSON Pointer paths
The client object model
Binding Trailer 1
Language-independent conformance vectors.
A current document looks like this:
{
"idl_version": "0.1.0",
"interfaces": [
{
"id": "lock_witness",
"kind": "witness_args.lock",
"encoding": {
"id": "ckb-idl-linear-0.1.0"
},
"fields": [
{
"name": "signature",
"type": "secp256k1_sig",
"wire_type": "bytes_fixed_65",
"required": true,
"description": "Signature authorizing the spend"
}
]
}
]
}
type may carry wallet-facing semantic meaning, while wire_type tells generic clients how the value is structurally encoded.
For example:
type: secp256k1_sig
wire_type: bytes_fixed_65
2. The Rust derive type registry is now larger
The original implementation supports u8, u32, u64, Vec<u8>, [u8; 33], [u8; 65], [u8; 64]. The current implementation now supports:
u8
u16
u32
u64
u128
[u8; N], where N > 0
Vec<u8>
typed Vec<T>
trailing Option<T>
nested structs
explicitly tagged unions
Typed vectors currently support fixed-size element types. Vec<u8> remains a length-prefixed byte string rather than vector<uint8>.
Semantic annotations can be applied explicitly:
#[derive(CkbWitness)]
pub struct Witness {
#[witness(
type = "secp256k1_sig",
description = "Signature authorizing the spend"
)]
pub signature: [u8; 65],
pub nonce: u64,
}
The semantic registry currently includes values such as:
secp256k1_sig
secp256k1_pubkey
schnorr_sig
blake2b_hash
Authors can also use namespaced custom semantic labels while preserving a supported structural wire type.
Nested Structs
Reusable inner witness structures can derive CkbInnerWitness. Their complete nested field definitions appear recursively in the exported IDL.
Tagged Unions
Authorization choices and similar enums can derive CkbWitnessUnion.
Union tags must be explicit:
#[witness(tag = 1)]
They are never inferred from declaration order. This makes reordering Rust source unable to silently change the wire ABI.
Duplicate tags are rejected, and exported variants are sorted by tag.
Optional fields
Optional fields use Rust Option<T> and must appear at the end of their containing record.
Their wire behavior is trailing exhaustion:
buffer exhausted → Optional(None)
bytes remain → Optional(Some(value))
This makes an absent Option<Vec<u8>> distinguishable from a present empty byte string, because present bytes still contain a four-byte zero-length prefix.
3. Recursive IDL export is now explicit
The derive macro generates runtime decoding and static schema metadata during compilation.
For flat witnesses it can still produce a convenient local artifact, but recursive deployment artifacts use the host-side ckb-idl-export crate.
A contract adds:
// examples/export_idl.rs
ckb_idl_export::export_idl_main!(my_lock::witness::Witness);
Then exports the authoritative document with:
cargo run --example export_idl -- artifacts/my-lock.idl.json
This separation is intentional:
The on-chain script remains no_std.
The host exporter can recursively traverse schemas.
Nested structs, vectors and unions are fully represented.
Deployment does not accidentally hash an incomplete or stale macro-side file.
The exporter writes RFC 8785 canonical JSON directly.
4. The Rust client now supports the complete 0.1 object model
The client repository has moved under the new GitHub organization:
ckb-idl-client
It now supports:
Exact-byte registry fetching.
RFC 8785 canonicalization verification.
Binding Trailer 1 verification.
Recursive document validation.
Structural wire_type dispatch.
All 0.1 scalar types.
Fixed bytes.
Typed vectors.
Nested structs.
Tagged unions.
Trailing optionals.
Stable errors and nested paths.
Witness decoding.
Witness encoding.
Decoded witnesses are represented as an ordered WitnessObject.
This matters because field order is part of the linear wire encoding, even though callers also need object-style lookup by name.
A wallet can decode:
let object = client.decode_lock_witness(&document, witness_lock_bytes)?;
if let Some(value) = object.get("authorization") {
// render or inspect the authorization
}
It can also construct an object and encode it:
let witness = client.encode_lock_witness(&document, &object)?;
The encoder rejects:
Missing fields.
Unknown fields.
Incorrect field order.
Incorrect logical types.
Incorrect fixed-byte lengths.
Unknown union tags.
Tag/name disagreement.
Invalid optional gaps.
Empty typed vectors.
Stable errors
Errors expose both a stable category and an RFC 6901-style path.
Examples:
field_too_short at /signature
field_too_short at /authorization/value/signature
field_too_short at /signatures/1
invalid_document at /interfaces/0/fields/1/type
trailing_bytes at ""
These categories and paths are tested against the language-independent specification fixtures.
The client now passes the normative valid, malformed, canonicalization and recursive conformance vectors.
5. The commitment format is now parseable and versioned
The original experiment appended only:
SHA-256(idl.json)
That was simple, but it did not provide a domain-specific marker, version or room for future binding formats.
IDL 0.1.0 now uses Binding Trailer 1:
idl_digest = SHA-256(canonical_idl_bytes)
payload =
version_u8
|| flags_u8
|| idl_digest_32
code_cell_data =
executable
|| payload
|| payload_length_u32_le
|| magic_8
Current constants are:
version = 1
flags = 0
payload length = 34
magic = "CKBIDL\0\0"
total trailer length = 46 bytes
The complete IDL does not go on-chain. Only the 46-byte trailer is appended to the executable.
For scripts using a data-based hash type, the resulting CKB code hash covers:
executable + IDL binding trailer
Therefore, changing either the executable or its committed interface changes the deployed script identity.
6. There is now a standalone commitment CLI
A new repository now exists under the organization:
ckb-idl-cli
It provides the ckb-idl command with four operations:
ckb-idl validate
ckb-idl bind
ckb-idl inspect
ckb-idl verify
Validate
ckb-idl validate --idl artifacts/my-lock.idl.json
This validates:
UTF-8 JSON.
A single complete JSON value.
RFC 8785 canonical bytes.
IDL version and interface schema.
Recursive field structure.
Semantic and structural type rules.
It does not rewrite the source document.
Bind
ckb-idl bind \
--executable build/release/my-lock \
--idl artifacts/my-lock.idl.json \
--out-dir dist/my-lock
This creates:
dist/my-lock/
├── my-lock
├── my-lock.idl.json
└── my-lock.binding.json
The output contains:
The executable with Binding Trailer 1.
An exact byte-for-byte copy of the frozen IDL.
A deterministic canonical binding manifest.
The manifest records:
IDL version and encoding.
IDL SHA-256.
Clean executable CKB data hash.
Bound code-data CKB hash.
Clean and bound byte lengths.
Trailer version, flags, length and magic.
Safety
The CLI:
Never modifies source files.
Refuses existing output directories.
Refuses to bind an already-bound executable.
Preserves executable permissions.
Writes into a staging directory.
Re-reads and verifies every staged artifact.
Publishes the complete directory atomically.
Cleans temporary state after failure.
Produces deterministic output for identical inputs.
The standalone core commands and their tests are implemented. Integration into the reference deployer is currently underway.
7. More realistic reference scripts
The original article used simple-lock and timelock-lock.
The reference workspace now includes:
simple-lock — length-prefixed preimage bytes.
timelock-lock — signature, timestamp and auxiliary payload.
hash-commitment-lock — semantic hash fields.
multisig-threshold-lock — typed vectors of fixed-size signatures.
authorization-choice-lock — nested structures and explicitly tagged authorization unions.
optional-memo-lock — trailing optional wallet-visible bytes.
These scripts were useful for discovering protocol constraints that were not obvious from the original flat examples.
For example:
Nested records need explicit boundary rules.
Typed vectors need fixed-size element restrictions.
Union tags cannot safely depend on declaration order.
Optional nested containers require additional framing and are therefore excluded from the current encoding.
Wallet-facing semantic types must remain separate from structural wire types.
Host exporters are being added to all IDL-enabled contracts, along with Makefile targets for:
make export-idl
make package
make test-bound
make deploy
The next integration milestone is to:
Package all reference scripts.
Replace the old raw-digest deployer.
Deploy the already-bound executable unchanged.
Execute at least one bound script in ckb-testtool.
Verify the deployed output-data hash against the generated manifest.
This work is in progress rather than complete.
8. The project now has a GitHub organization
I created the ckb-idl GitHub organization to separate the protocol and coordinated implementations from my unrelated personal repositories.
The specification, client and CLI are now being consolidated there. The derive/export crates and reference workspace are also being prepared for coordinated versioning and releases.
The intention is to publish mutually compatible versions of:
ckb-idl-types
ckb-idl-derive
ckb-idl-export
ckb-idl-client
ckb-idl-cli
The CLI will ultimately be installable with:
cargo install ckb-idl-cli
Release binaries and checksums are also planned.
9. What about Molecule?
CKB IDL is not intended to replace Molecule.
Molecule already provides a widely used binary schema and encoding system in the CKB ecosystem. IDL is aimed at a different layer:
Molecule:
how bytes are structurally serialized
IDL:
which script interface is being supplied,
where it belongs,
what fields mean to wallets,
and how to discover and verify that interface
The roadmap includes:
A Molecule encoding profile.
Generating IDL documents from .mol schemas.
Adding wallet-facing field descriptions and semantic annotations that Molecule itself does not carry.
Allowing existing Molecule-based scripts to participate in registry discovery without rewriting their contracts around the Rust derive.
Molecule support is important for broad ecosystem adoption, but it is not required to validate the registry and discovery model with the current linear-profile reference scripts.
10. The registry direction is clearer
The original post ended with uncertainty about where IDLs should live.
My current conclusion is that the protocol should not depend on one trusted registry.
A registry returns candidate bytes. The client independently verifies those bytes against the deployed code-cell commitment.
The registry I am considering is something between:
npm
+ OpenZeppelin
+ a script-interface explorer
From npm:
Publisher namespaces.
Versions.
Immutable release artifacts.
Deprecation and yanking.
Installation and publication tooling.
From OpenZeppelin:
Curated reusable scripts.
Security and audit metadata.
Documentation.
Integration examples.
Recommended usage patterns.
From an explorer:
Resolve an unfamiliar script identity to its interface.
Show deployed versions and code-cell evidence.
Display IDL fields and semantic types.
Generate transaction-builder examples.
It does not need to become a general transaction or block explorer.
The registry should support at least:
Exact frozen IDL storage.
Binding manifests.
Script identity and deployment metadata.
Source, license and audit links.
Search by code hash, name, category and semantic type.
Transaction-builder snippets.
Chain-verified deployment evidence.
Separate treatment of deployed scripts and undeployed reusable templates.
11. What is still unfinished?
The main remaining work before calling IDL 0.1.0 ready includes:
Complete reference-script package/deploy/execute evidence.
Replace local and floating dependencies with coordinated releases.
Finalize and test resource limits.
Publish mutually compatible Rust crates.
Finish commitment-tool installation and release packaging.
Freeze the final specification fixtures and tag v0.1.0.
Deferred work includes:
Script args.
Other WitnessArgs fields.
Type-script and cell-data interfaces.
Molecule encoding.
TypeScript parity.
Type-hash-aware code-cell versioning.
Rich signing metadata.
Additional binding-trailer versions.
The next major phase is the registry and reusable-script ecosystem around it.
Does the separation between IDL protocol, commitment tooling and registry discovery make sense?
Which existing CKB scripts should receive manually authored IDLs first?
How important is Molecule-to-IDL support for the first registry MVP?
Which wallet or transaction-building workflows should the first integration target?
Should reusable undeployed script templates live beside deployed, chain-verified releases, or in a separate registry section?
Are there existing script deployment tools that should consume the deterministic binding manifest directly?
The repositories are available for review, and I will continue publishing implementation progress while the remaining deployment integration is completed.
Thanks again to everyone who commented on the first post and helped sharpen the direction.

- let wallets validate witness bytes before submission

Since then, I have spent time testing the idea against more realistic scripts, expanding the supported type system, separating the protocol from its implementations, and building the missing deployment tooling.

The project is now simply called CKB IDL rather than LS-IDL. IDL 0.1.0 still supports only WitnessArgs.Lock, but the longer-term direction includes other script interfaces, so “Lock Script IDL” had become unnecessarily restrictive.

This post is an update on what has changed, what now works, and what I intend building next.

The original problem

CKB scripts are highly programmable, but wallets and transaction builders do not have a standard machine-readable way to discover the witness format expected by an unfamiliar script. “Unfamiliar” in this context refers to a machine having access to nothing but the code hash of the code cell that holds the script.

This means that integration today requires prior knowledge of the script, and when this knowledge is wrong, errors are often discovered only during VM execution.

The goal of CKB IDL remains:

script identity
- discover interface
- verify interface against deployed code
- construct or inspect witness safely

The registry is used for discovery, but it is not trusted as the authority. The deployed code cell commits to the exact IDL bytes.

1. IDL Specification

The protocol is no longer defined implicitly by the Rust derive implementation. There is now a dedicated specification repository: https://github.com/ckb-idl/ckb-idl-spec

It defines:

  • The IDL 0.1.0 JSON Schema
  • The interfaces document model
  • The witness_args.lock interface
  • The ckb-idl-linear-0.1.0 encoding profile
  • Structural and semantic types
  • Nested structs and tagged unions
  • Optional-field behaviour
  • RFC 8785 canonicalization
  • Stable error categories are JSON Pointer paths
  • The client object model
  • Binding Trailer 1
  • Language-independent conformance vectors.

A current document looks like this:

{
  "idl_version": "0.1.0",
  "interfaces": [
    {
      "id": "lock_witness",
      "kind": "witness_args.lock",
      "encoding": {
        "id": "ckb-idl-linear-0.1.0"
      },
      "fields": [
        {
          "name": "signature",
          "type": "secp256k1_sig",
          "wire_type": "bytes_fixed_65",
          "required": true,
          "description": "Signature authorizing the spend"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

type may carry wallet-facing semantic meaning, while wire_type tells generic clients how the value is structurally encoded.

For example:

type:      secp256k1_sig
wire_type: bytes_fixed_65

2. The Rust derive type registry is now larger

The original implementation supports u8, u32, u64, Vec<u8>, [u8; 33], [u8; 65], [u8; 64]. The current implementation now supports:

u8
u16
u32
u64
u128
[u8; N], where N > 0
Vec<u8>
typed Vec<T>
trailing Option<T>
nested structs
explicitly tagged unions

Typed vectors currently support fixed-size element types. Vec<u8> remains a length-prefixed byte string rather than vector<uint8>.

Semantic annotations can be applied explicitly:

#[derive(CkbWitness)]
pub struct Witness {
    #[witness(
        type = "secp256k1_sig",
        description = "Signature authorizing the spend"
    )]
    pub signature: [u8; 65],

    pub nonce: u64,
}

The semantic registry currently includes values such as:

  • secp256k1_sig
  • secp256k1_pubkey
  • schnorr_sig
  • blake2b_hash

Authors can also use namespaced custom semantic labels while preserving a supported structural wire type.

Nested Structs

Reusable inner witness structures can derive CkbInnerWitness. Their complete nested field definitions appear recursively in the exported IDL.

Tagged Unions

Authorization choices and similar enums can derive CkbWitnessUnion.

Union tags must be explicit:

#[witness(tag = 1)]

They are never inferred from declaration order. This makes reordering Rust source unable to silently change the wire ABI.

Duplicate tags are rejected, and exported variants are sorted by tag.

Optional fields

Optional fields use Rust Option<T> and must appear at the end of their containing record.

Their wire behavior is trailing exhaustion:

buffer exhausted → Optional(None)
bytes remain      → Optional(Some(value))

This makes an absent Option<Vec<u8>> distinguishable from a present empty byte string, because present bytes still contain a four-byte zero-length prefix.

3. Recursive IDL export is now explicit

The derive macro generates runtime decoding and static schema metadata during compilation.

For flat witnesses it can still produce a convenient local artifact, but recursive deployment artifacts use the host-side ckb-idl-export crate.

A contract adds:

// examples/export_idl.rs

ckb_idl_export::export_idl_main!(my_lock::witness::Witness);

Then exports the authoritative document with:

cargo run --example export_idl -- artifacts/my-lock.idl.json

This separation is intentional:

  • The on-chain script remains no_std.
  • The host exporter can recursively traverse schemas.
  • Nested structs, vectors and unions are fully represented.
  • Deployment does not accidentally hash an incomplete or stale macro-side file.

The exporter writes RFC 8785 canonical JSON directly.

4. The Rust client now supports the complete 0.1 object model

The client repository has moved under the new GitHub organization:

  • ckb-idl-client

It now supports:

  • Exact-byte registry fetching.
  • RFC 8785 canonicalization verification.
  • Binding Trailer 1 verification.
  • Recursive document validation.
  • Structural wire_type dispatch.
  • All 0.1 scalar types.
  • Fixed bytes.
  • Typed vectors.
  • Nested structs.
  • Tagged unions.
  • Trailing optionals.
  • Stable errors and nested paths.
  • Witness decoding.
  • Witness encoding.

Decoded witnesses are represented as an ordered WitnessObject.

This matters because field order is part of the linear wire encoding, even though callers also need object-style lookup by name.

A wallet can decode:

let object = client.decode_lock_witness(&document, witness_lock_bytes)?;

if let Some(value) = object.get("authorization") {
    // render or inspect the authorization
}

It can also construct an object and encode it:

let witness = client.encode_lock_witness(&document, &object)?;

The encoder rejects:

  • Missing fields.
  • Unknown fields.
  • Incorrect field order.
  • Incorrect logical types.
  • Incorrect fixed-byte lengths.
  • Unknown union tags.
  • Tag/name disagreement.
  • Invalid optional gaps.
  • Empty typed vectors.

Stable errors

Errors expose both a stable category and an RFC 6901-style path.

Examples:

field_too_short at /signature
field_too_short at /authorization/value/signature
field_too_short at /signatures/1
invalid_document at /interfaces/0/fields/1/type
trailing_bytes at ""

These categories and paths are tested against the language-independent specification fixtures.

The client now passes the normative valid, malformed, canonicalization and recursive conformance vectors.

5. The commitment format is now parseable and versioned

The original experiment appended only:

SHA-256(idl.json)

That was simple, but it did not provide a domain-specific marker, version or room for future binding formats.

IDL 0.1.0 now uses Binding Trailer 1:

idl_digest = SHA-256(canonical_idl_bytes)

payload =
    version_u8
    || flags_u8
    || idl_digest_32

code_cell_data =
    executable
    || payload
    || payload_length_u32_le
    || magic_8

Current constants are:

version = 1
flags = 0
payload length = 34
magic = "CKBIDL\0\0"
total trailer length = 46 bytes

The complete IDL does not go on-chain. Only the 46-byte trailer is appended to the executable.

For scripts using a data-based hash type, the resulting CKB code hash covers:

executable + IDL binding trailer

Therefore, changing either the executable or its committed interface changes the deployed script identity.

6. There is now a standalone commitment CLI

A new repository now exists under the organization:

  • ckb-idl-cli

It provides the ckb-idl command with four operations:

ckb-idl validate
ckb-idl bind
ckb-idl inspect
ckb-idl verify

Validate

ckb-idl validate --idl artifacts/my-lock.idl.json

This validates:

  • UTF-8 JSON.
  • A single complete JSON value.
  • RFC 8785 canonical bytes.
  • IDL version and interface schema.
  • Recursive field structure.
  • Semantic and structural type rules.

It does not rewrite the source document.

Bind

ckb-idl bind \
  --executable build/release/my-lock \
  --idl artifacts/my-lock.idl.json \
  --out-dir dist/my-lock

This creates:

dist/my-lock/
├── my-lock
├── my-lock.idl.json
└── my-lock.binding.json

The output contains:

  • The executable with Binding Trailer 1.
  • An exact byte-for-byte copy of the frozen IDL.
  • A deterministic canonical binding manifest.

The manifest records:

  • IDL version and encoding.
  • IDL SHA-256.
  • Clean executable CKB data hash.
  • Bound code-data CKB hash.
  • Clean and bound byte lengths.
  • Trailer version, flags, length and magic.

Safety

The CLI:

  • Never modifies source files.
  • Refuses existing output directories.
  • Refuses to bind an already-bound executable.
  • Preserves executable permissions.
  • Writes into a staging directory.
  • Re-reads and verifies every staged artifact.
  • Publishes the complete directory atomically.
  • Cleans temporary state after failure.
  • Produces deterministic output for identical inputs.

The standalone core commands and their tests are implemented. Integration into the reference deployer is currently underway.

7. More realistic reference scripts

The original article used simple-lock and timelock-lock.

The reference workspace now includes:

  • simple-lock — length-prefixed preimage bytes.
  • timelock-lock — signature, timestamp and auxiliary payload.
  • hash-commitment-lock — semantic hash fields.
  • multisig-threshold-lock — typed vectors of fixed-size signatures.
  • authorization-choice-lock — nested structures and explicitly tagged authorization unions.
  • optional-memo-lock — trailing optional wallet-visible bytes.

These scripts were useful for discovering protocol constraints that were not obvious from the original flat examples.

For example:

  • Nested records need explicit boundary rules.
  • Typed vectors need fixed-size element restrictions.
  • Union tags cannot safely depend on declaration order.
  • Optional nested containers require additional framing and are therefore excluded from the current encoding.
  • Wallet-facing semantic types must remain separate from structural wire types.

Host exporters are being added to all IDL-enabled contracts, along with Makefile targets for:

make export-idl
make package
make test-bound
make deploy

The next integration milestone is to:

  1. Package all reference scripts.
  2. Replace the old raw-digest deployer.
  3. Deploy the already-bound executable unchanged.
  4. Execute at least one bound script in ckb-testtool.
  5. Verify the deployed output-data hash against the generated manifest.

This work is in progress rather than complete.

8. The project now has a GitHub organization

I created the ckb-idl GitHub organization to separate the protocol and coordinated implementations from my unrelated personal repositories.

The specification, client and CLI are now being consolidated there. The derive/export crates and reference workspace are also being prepared for coordinated versioning and releases.

The intention is to publish mutually compatible versions of:

ckb-idl-types
ckb-idl-derive
ckb-idl-export
ckb-idl-client
ckb-idl-cli

The CLI will ultimately be installable with:

cargo install ckb-idl-cli

Release binaries and checksums are also planned.

9. What about Molecule?

CKB IDL is not intended to replace Molecule.

Molecule already provides a widely used binary schema and encoding system in the CKB ecosystem. IDL is aimed at a different layer:

Molecule:
how bytes are structurally serialized

IDL:
which script interface is being supplied,
where it belongs,
what fields mean to wallets,
and how to discover and verify that interface

The roadmap includes:

  • A Molecule encoding profile.
  • Generating IDL documents from .mol schemas.
  • Adding wallet-facing field descriptions and semantic annotations that Molecule itself does not carry.
  • Allowing existing Molecule-based scripts to participate in registry discovery without rewriting their contracts around the Rust derive.

Molecule support is important for broad ecosystem adoption, but it is not required to validate the registry and discovery model with the current linear-profile reference scripts.

10. The registry direction is clearer

The original post ended with uncertainty about where IDLs should live.

My current conclusion is that the protocol should not depend on one trusted registry.

A registry returns candidate bytes. The client independently verifies those bytes against the deployed code-cell commitment.

The registry I am considering is something between:

npm
+ OpenZeppelin
+ a script-interface explorer

From npm:

  • Publisher namespaces.
  • Versions.
  • Immutable release artifacts.
  • Deprecation and yanking.
  • Installation and publication tooling.

From OpenZeppelin:

  • Curated reusable scripts.
  • Security and audit metadata.
  • Documentation.
  • Integration examples.
  • Recommended usage patterns.

From an explorer:

  • Resolve an unfamiliar script identity to its interface.
  • Show deployed versions and code-cell evidence.
  • Display IDL fields and semantic types.
  • Generate transaction-builder examples.

It does not need to become a general transaction or block explorer.

The registry should support at least:

  • Exact frozen IDL storage.
  • Binding manifests.
  • Script identity and deployment metadata.
  • Source, license and audit links.
  • Search by code hash, name, category and semantic type.
  • Transaction-builder snippets.
  • Chain-verified deployment evidence.
  • Separate treatment of deployed scripts and undeployed reusable templates.

11. What is still unfinished?

The main remaining work before calling IDL 0.1.0 ready includes:

  • Complete reference-script package/deploy/execute evidence.
  • Replace local and floating dependencies with coordinated releases.
  • Finalize and test resource limits.
  • Publish mutually compatible Rust crates.
  • Finish commitment-tool installation and release packaging.
  • Freeze the final specification fixtures and tag v0.1.0.

Deferred work includes:

  • Script args.
  • Other WitnessArgs fields.
  • Type-script and cell-data interfaces.
  • Molecule encoding.
  • TypeScript parity.
  • Type-hash-aware code-cell versioning.
  • Rich signing metadata.
  • Additional binding-trailer versions.

The next major phase is the registry and reusable-script ecosystem around it.

  1. Does the separation between IDL protocol, commitment tooling and registry discovery make sense?
  2. Which existing CKB scripts should receive manually authored IDLs first?
  3. How important is Molecule-to-IDL support for the first registry MVP?
  4. Which wallet or transaction-building workflows should the first integration target?
  5. Should reusable undeployed script templates live beside deployed, chain-verified releases, or in a separate registry section?
  6. Are there existing script deployment tools that should consume the deterministic binding manifest directly?

The repositories are available for review, and I will continue publishing implementation progress while the remaining deployment integration is completed.

Thanks again to everyone who commented on the first post and helped sharpen the direction.
